hops.title: Why there is still room for dessert
hops.text: You are too full for another forkful of pasta, yet two minutes later a cookie looks fine. Barbara Rolls and colleagues tested this in 1984. Their study of 48 volunteers compared two four-course lunches: one served the same food four times, the other four different foods. With variety, people ate 60% more calories, mostly in the third and fourth courses. The rated pleasantness of each food fell quickly as it was eaten, while uneaten foods held up. Eating a savory food lowered the appeal of other savory foods more than sweet ones, and the reverse held for sweet. The food just eaten lost the most appeal.

sources.citation: Rolls BJ, Van Duijvenvoorde PM, Rolls ET (1984). Pleasantness changes and food intake in a varied four-course meal. Appetite 5(4):337-348.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A half-eaten plate of pasta pushed slightly back beside a small plate with a chocolate-chip cookie and sliced strawberries.
image.caption: Eating one food lowers its value, while a food of a different kind stays appealing.

hops.afterHeading: Hunger: a fuel gauge and two opposed groups of neurons
hops.title: Why some Labradors are so keen on food
hops.text: About 22% of UK pet Labrador retrievers carry a 14-base-pair deletion in the POMC gene. The deletion stops that copy of the gene from making two of its usual peptides, one of which activates MC4R, the stop button, much as alpha-MSH does. Each copy was linked to about 1.9 kilograms more body weight on average. Three hours after a standard meal, carriers spent longer investigating a perforated box with a sausage inside than noncarriers did. In one assistance-dog breeding program, about three quarters of 81 Labradors carried the deletion. The authors suggest that dogs keen on food may be easier to train with food rewards, though that is not proven.

sources.citation: Raffan E et al. (2016). A Deletion in the Canine POMC Gene Is Associated with Weight and Appetite in Obesity-Prone Labrador Retriever Dogs. Cell Metabolism 23(5):893-900.
Dittmann MT, Raffan E et al. (2024). Low resting metabolic rate and increased hunger due to beta-MSH and beta-endorphin deletion in a canine model. Science Advances 10(10):eadj3823.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A golden Labrador retriever in a plain harness staring closely at a sausage sealed inside a clear perforated plastic box.
image.caption: Labradors carrying a POMC deletion spent longer investigating a box with a sausage sealed inside.

hops.afterHeading: In addiction, wanting can grow while liking does not
hops.title: Three thousand lever presses for a dose without significantly higher liking ratings
hops.text: In 1991, researchers at the National Institute on Drug Abuse asked five volunteers with histories of heroin use to work for a weekday injection. The price was 3,000 lever presses: 30 rounds of 100, with a brief light after each round. Placebo did not keep anyone pressing. At the lowest morphine dose tested, four of the five kept responding. Yet on their questionnaires, grouped liking ratings at that dose showed no statistically significant increase over placebo. The drug kept their behavior going even though the group's reported liking did not rise significantly above placebo.

sources.citation: Lamb RJ, Preston KL, Schindler CW, Meisch RA, Davis F, Katz JL, Henningfield JE, Goldberg SR (1991). The reinforcing and subjective effects of morphine in post-addicts: a dose-response study. Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics 259(3):1165-1173.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage laboratory box with a single brass lever and a small glowing amber light on a wooden desk.
image.caption: Four of five volunteers kept pressing for low-dose morphine, while group liking ratings were not significantly above placebo.
